sn20.7:1.2: The Dasārahas were probably the people known in Sanskrit as the Daśārṇa of the western Vindhya mountains. | The _mudiṅga_ is a double-headed drum known today as _mridangam_, which is still widely used in southern India. It is named for the paste (“mud”, today called the _karanai_) applied to one of the heads that gives it its distinctive snare-like tone (_chapu_). The skin is attached with a wooden rim tightened with leather straps. | _Āṇaka_ is another name for what is said to be a large military drum, which might be named after _āṇi_ in the sense of “tuning peg”, a feature of the modern _mardala_. However, in this case, the context requires that the _āṇi_ be a plug for patching the shell, after which the drum was named “Plugger”.
sn20.7:1.4: The _pokkhara_ is the “drumskin”. The _phalaka_ is the “wooden shell”, a single hollowed-out log from which the _mridangam_ is constructed.
sn20.7:1.6: Such discourses by the Buddha himself, which are also referred to at [an2.47:1.5](), [an5.79:5.2](), and [sn55.53:2.2](), contrast with the frivolous poetry of outsiders. Unsurprisingly, the Vedas take the opposite stance, for there it is the poets whose insight is “deep” (Rig Veda 2.21.4, 8.8.2; Atharva Veda 4.26.3). | “Deep” (_gambhīra_) emphasizes substantial understanding rather than surface appearance ([an4.104]()). | “Deep in meaning” (_gambhīrattha_) implies both richness in textual implications, as well as profundity of purpose. | “Transcendent” (_lokuttara_) emphasizes that the teachings lead beyond the mundane concerns of worldly life. | The phrase “dealing with emptiness” (_suññatappaṭisaṁyutta_) is itself rich in implications. It locates the Buddha’s teachings in relation to his rejection of the Vedic _ātman_ ([mn43:33.1]()), while also pointing to the practice of seclusion and solitude in developing meditation ([mn121]()). Ultimately it refers to Nibbāna as the emptiness of greed, hate, and delusion ([mn43:37.4]()).
